claims.text: Corrosion behavior of pre-exposed Q235 steel is governed by its native, fine-grained iron oxide layer.
At room temperature, the native iron oxide layer acts as an effective barrier against salt-induced degradation.
At 700–900 °C, the native oxide layer undergoes microstructural destabilization, such as phase transformation or spallation.
High-temperature destabilization of the oxide causes loss of protection and increased corrosion.
As-received Q235 mild steel has a naturally formed iron oxide film resulting from ambient exposure.
Controlled annealing can stabilize and densify the native iron oxide layer.
Oxide-layer coherence, grain size, and adhesion govern its barrier effect against corrosive species.
A dense and adherent native iron oxide layer prevents ingress of aggressive ions from salt solution at ambient temperature.
Thermal energy at high temperature triggers oxide grain growth, phase transitions, or spallation.
The thermally induced oxide changes compromise scale integrity and permit rapid corrosive attack.
At room temperature, annealed Q235 samples will have lower corrosion rates, reduced mass change, and better-preserved oxide microstructure than untreated samples.
At 700–900 °C, even annealed samples will exhibit accelerated corrosion and disrupted oxide integrity.
The proposed mechanism applies only in the absence of additional protective coatings or significant alloy modifications.
Mechanical cleaning or chemical etching that removes or substantially modifies the native oxide may invalidate the proposed behavior.
Failure of annealing to improve room-temperature corrosion resistance, or absence of oxide destabilization at high temperature, would falsify the proposed oxide-governed mechanism.
